Drugs are a malignant black that chemically destroy everything you hold sacred in life if abused long enough. I've regretted being stupid enough to momentarily forget that ever since.

Do I think, theoretically, that he can change? Yes. Going off what other people who've struggled with substance abuse have told me (I live in Central Ohio, he's far from the only addict I know), he'll probably have urges for the rest of his life regardless of what his actions are. That part can't be changed. But can he somehow gain the strength to fight those battles, and win every one? If I were in his shoes, I wouldn't be able to do it, and I'm probably one of the most emotionally iron-willed individuals I know. And no one can do it for him. And if he were ever going to turn his life around, it probably should've been when he became a father. But miracles can happen, even when it's so unlikely that I'd call them just that--a miracle.

However,

Do I tell people that I think he can change (other than on Voat where no one other than some three letter agency knows my name)? No. I usually try not to talk about him. And when I do, I say he's dead to me. I'll say he's dead to me even if he kicks his habit tomorrow and lives to not touch it for another fifty years. If I were a saint, maybe I'd say he has another chance. I'm not a saint, and I can't predict the future. I have plenty of problems myself, and not nearly enough altruism to give him any hope of another chance from me.

 

Now, that big and rather personal block of text being said, that's just one aspect (albeit a large one) of one individual I know. "Do you believe people can change?" is a pretty broad question, my cousin's history of substance abuse was just the first place my mind went is all. People change all the time if you look at it in that sense. If you don't mind me talking about myself, I got plenty of examples of change over the years. I used to hate and fear exercise, now I love it and can't function without moving heavy things around at least every other day. I used to think appearances shouldn't matter, now I judge most things in life on face value. I used to be a little liberal as a young kid, rode the libertarian high off the whole Ron Paul revolution thing around 2008, and now I think people have too much freedom and that whites need their own ethnostate. If I were to bet money on it I'd say I'll eventually get tired of being a racist too and move on to something else in the future. If it's happened before, who's to say it won't happen again?

And if you want to look at the question broader than that, then biologically everyone changes everyday. Granted that's kinda common knowledge and a bit of a letdown of an answer. But maybe worth mentioning.

Anyway, if I have to give a yes or no answer, then

TL;DR Yes, they can. It just doesn't always happen.

Absolutely, and I can even explain in detail why they tend not to.

Part of it: what defines an adult tends to be a decision that they know what they need in order to survive... they don't need to latch on to a caretaker to learn from anymore.

Part of it: its takes a well informed and introspective process in order to shift perspective and re-evaluate past events.

If you want to know more, Tad James has a good book called timeline therapy that provides an intro into manipulating one's core values. It is the tip of the iceberg, however I have found that even claiming people can change at all doesn't go over well, because that would require acceptance that they can change, which is truly the heart of the issue.

Source: I've helped people change dramatically for money.
